newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican rebels vow to attack if elections are dirty.
newsitem.headline: Mexican rebels vow to attack if elections are dirty.
newsitem.dateline: IN THE MOUNTAINS OF OAXACA, Mexico 1997-06-30

text.p: Marxist rebels in Mexico warned the government they would launch fresh attacks against it if the ruling party resorted to wdespread fraud in next week's national elections.

In an interview with Reuters a year after the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) first appeared, EPR military leaders in this southern Mexican state on Sunday pledged to uphold a unilateral ceasefire through next week's key mid-term poll.

But they vowed to resume military attacks similar to those it launched last year in several Mexican states if the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party used fraud to prolong its 68-year hold on power.
"If there is fraud in the elections, we would support the people in whatever way they want, including militarily," said EPR Commander Francisco, his face covered in the group's trademark brown hood.
"If villages decide to rebel, and the army cracks down on them, then it is our obligation to join the people and respond in a military manner."
Mexico's ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) faces its worst defeat ever during Sunday's key mid-term elections.

The party, which has at times used fraud to stay in power since 1929, is almost sure to lose the race for Mexico City mayor and may lose control of the lower house of Congress for the first time ever.
Rebels acknowledged the elections, which the government has promised will be Mexico's cleanest to date, would help promote democracy in Mexico.

But they said clean elections would not be a good enough reason for them to give up their struggle to overthrow the government of President Ernesto Zedillo, which the EPR says is not doing enough to rid Mexico of poverty and inequality.

"Democracy is not just depositing ballots on July 6. Democracy is carrying out the will of the people on a day-to-day basis," said Commander Vicente, another member of the group's self-styled General Command.

Singing a rebel hymn in hushed tones to avoid detection by army troops, dozens of armed guerrillas gathered in a makeshift camp hidden in tropical forest to pay homage to 17 leftist peasants killed in a police massacre on June 28, 1995.
The camp was some 11 hours by mountain road and on foot from the state capital, Oaxaca, and reporters were blindfolded for part of the journey.
The ERP claims to have killed 150 soldiers and policemen since its appearance exactly a year after the massacre. Officially, EPR attacks have killed about 30 people.
